posts.text: 1w The clock for a review request starts at the door. A checkout date tells you when money changed hands. It does not tell you whether a customer has received the product, let alone experienced it. When a review request fires while the parcel is still in transit, you are not collecting product feedback. You are inviting delivery frustration into a retention moment. Use two conditions: → confirmed delivery → enough time to use the product The second condition changes by category. For many physical goods, 7 to 14 days after confirmed delivery is a reasonable starting point. Then stop the sequence once the customer responds. Trigger off the event. Not the schedule. posts.text: 1w A customer pays. Their card is charged. But the order never reaches fulfillment. No pick ticket. No shipment. Then the support ticket arrives, and someone has to rebuild the order or issue a refund. This is rarely a warehouse problem. It is usually a blast-radius problem. When multiple stores share one account-level webhook endpoint and event scope, a configuration change for one store can interrupt order events for all of them. The better pattern is store-level isolation: • one endpoint per store • one event scope per store • one clear owner per store

posts.text: 2w An alert can save your chargeback ratio and still cost you more than the dispute. On paper, it looks like a win: • the dispute never reaches the processor • the ratio stays cleaner But that is only one part of the cost.
